name: anomaly
description: Outlier-detection arithmetic computed from the actual definitions: the k-th nearest-neighbour distance, the LOF ratio of local reachability densities, the Mahalanobis form and its covariance ellipse, a real Isolation Forest with Liu's c(n) path-length normalisation, a Gaussian-kernel one-class level set, rank-r reconstruction error, and the full threshold sweep of a scored labelled set into ROC, PR and confusion counts. Functions are available in the expression sandbox after importing this domain. Importing a domain does NOT require unsafe: true.
honesty_note: THE DATA IS SYNTHETIC AND PLANTED. Every dataset is drawn from a splitmix32 stream keyed on its string tag, and the 'anomalies' the detectors find were put there on purpose — the 'dense' strays, the 'ring' points in the hole, the flattened window in the signal, the 8% positive class in 'eval'. A lesson must say so on screen; claiming a detector discovered something the author planted is dishonest exactly where the lesson claims rigour. What is NOT invented is the SCORING: every score is the published definition, and scripts/check_anomaly_domain.py recomputes the statistical, distance, density and evaluation scores from scratch (the Isolation Forest's randomised trees are covered by invariants, not rebuilt) in NumPy and compares, so a drift in either the data or the arithmetic fails there.

implementation.purity: Every exported function is pure in its explicit arguments and reads no slider. A scene passes its sliders in — adLof('dense', i, k), adFenceZ(1, kz, contam) — which keeps the slider contract visible in the scene JSON and makes the whole library testable outside a browser. There is therefore no _init.
implementation.datasets: POINT-CLOUD TAGS -- blob, dense, ellip, ring -- are what a `tag` argument means; adN/adX/adY/adLabel and every 2-D scorer take one, and any other string hits a generic 100-point fallback that now warns. The metric and the eval set are NOT tags: they have their own accessors (adMetricN/adV/adPlanted and adEvalN/adScore/adEvalLabel). The metric is 1-D, 60 readings ~ N(50, 3), with `contam` of them replaced from a FIXED list in a FIXED order so the slider adds outliers one at a time and never reshuffles. 'blob' 180 ~ N(0, I) plus 12 uniform points rejected inside radius 3. 'dense' 90 points at (-2.2, 0) sd 0.25, 60 at (2.4, 0) sd 1.0, and 3 planted strays. 'ellip' 160 points on a ridge at 45 degrees with sd 2.2 along and 0.35 across, plus one point far ALONG the ridge (Euclidean-far, Mahalanobis-near) and one just ACROSS it (Euclidean-near, Mahalanobis-far). 'ring' 200 points on an annulus of radius 2.4 sd 0.22, plus 4 in the hole and 4 outside. 'eval' 400 points, 8% anomalous, scores drawn from overlapping clipped normals and pre-sorted descending so every threshold sweep is a prefix scan. A signal of 128 samples carries Fourier modes 2 and 3 plus noise, with samples 74-82 flattened to a constant level: a COLLECTIVE anomaly whose individual values stay inside the global range, so no z-score can see it.
implementation.quantiles: Linear-interpolation quantiles on an ascending array — NumPy's default. The MAD consistency constant is 1/Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 1.482602218505602, which is what makes 1.4826 * MAD an estimate of sigma for a normal.
implementation.lof: Breunig et al. 2000 as written: reach-dist_k(a,b) = max(k-distance(b), d(a,b)); lrd_k(a) = 1 / mean over N_k(a) of reach-dist_k(a,b); LOF_k(a) = mean over N_k(a) of lrd_k(b) / lrd_k(a). Neighbour lists are computed exactly (O(n^2 log n) once per dataset, n a couple of hundred) and truncated at k = 40.
implementation.isolation_forest: 100 trees, each on a subsample of 128 points drawn without replacement by a partial Fisher-Yates, each node splitting on a uniformly random axis at a uniform point in that axis's observed range, to depth ceil(log2 psi). A node that runs out of depth or points contributes c(size) for the subtree it did not build — Liu's estimator, not an approximation of it. c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n with H summed EXACTLY (the ln+gamma asymptotic is 27.6% low at n=3, and depth-capped trees credit c(size) at small leaves constantly; it is used only above n=100000), and the score is 2^(-E[h(x)] / c(psi)).
implementation.one_class_boundary: adKde is the Gaussian kernel density sum_j exp(-gamma ||x - x_j||^2) / n. adKdeQ is the nu-quantile of the training points' own densities, so declaring everything below it an outlier rejects APPROXIMATELY a nu fraction (an interpolated empirical quantile, with >= keeping ties, so nu = 0.1 rejects 0.101 of this training set). This is an operational analogue of a nu-SVM's nu, not the same guarantee: there nu is an upper bound on the training-error fraction and a lower bound on the support-vector fraction, and this is not an SVM. The drawn boundary is that level set, found by coarse scan plus 30 bisection steps along a ray; adKdeR gives the outer crossing and adKdeRin the inner one, so an annulus traces both walls. Only ONE crossing pair per ray is kept, so this traces a single annulus; when a high gamma fragments the level set into disconnected islands the extra crossings are dropped and the drawn curve is no longer the level set. This is the FULL-RANK version of the object a One-Class SVM approximates with a sparse set of support vectors, not a One-Class SVM; the lesson says so.
implementation.reconstruction: adRecon keeps the mean plus the r lowest Fourier modes — a linear autoencoder of a periodic signal, and a true bottleneck. The capacity story is visible in the numbers: at r=1 the anomaly window is LESS wrong than the rest of the signal (ratio 0.75, the detector is inverted); at r=3 the contrast peaks (ratio 1.98); by r=10 the model reconstructs the anomaly as well as it reconstructs the signal (ratio 0.95) and the detector is dead. adPcaErr is the rank-1 PCA reconstruction error of a 2-D cloud — the distance from the first principal axis, in closed form from the covariance.
implementation.evaluation: 'eval' is sorted descending by score once, so adConf's prefix scan is exact at every threshold and adAucRoc / adAucPr are single passes (trapezoid over every distinct operating point, and average precision respectively). adPrecBayes is the base-rate identity in closed form and consults no dataset at all: hold TPR and FPR fixed, slide pi, and precision collapses while ROC-AUC does not move.
implementation.concentration: adConc measures the curse of dimensionality instead of asserting it. For each dimension d, 120 points are drawn uniformly in the unit cube and each point's nearest and farthest neighbour are found exactly. The relative contrast (dmax - dmin) / dmin is what every distance-based detector depends on: it falls from 29.1 at d = 2 to 1.78 at d = 10, 0.96 at d = 20 and 0.44 at d = 64 — past about d = 20 the farthest neighbour is less than twice as far as the nearest, so 'far from its neighbours' has stopped distinguishing anything. At d = 1 the statistic is unstable (one near-coincident pair sends it into the thousands), so a scene should plot from d = 2. d is capped at 64.
implementation.caching: Three caches make the scenes run at frame rate. Per-point kernel densities are computed once per (tag, gamma), so colouring 200 points by membership is a lookup rather than 40,000 exponentials a frame. The one-class boundary is traced once per (tag, nu, gamma) at 128 angles (48-step scan plus 30 bisections each, about two million exponentials, ~70 ms) and read back by linear interpolation between angles; at an exact grid angle the value is the bisected one, which is why the checker's level-set assertion holds to 1e-6. Isolation path lengths are memoised on the exact coordinate pair (a tree is discontinuous at each split plane, so rounding could merge two genuinely different scores), because a heatmap asks for the same few hundred grid points every frame and each one walks 100 trees; the memo is cleared wholesale past 4096 entries so a sweeping query cannot leak.

verified_values.note: Asserted by scripts/check_anomaly_domain.py. If a change breaks one, the lesson's arithmetic is wrong, not the test.
verified_values.c_of_128: 8.866294 — the Isolation Forest path-length normalisation at psi = 128 (exact harmonic sum, not the ln+gamma asymptotic)
verified_values.masking: At contam = 8 the 3-sigma z-rule flags 2 of the 8 planted outliers; the 3-sigma MAD rule flags all 8. The mean has been dragged to 53.50 and sigma to 10.63, while the median holds at 50.34 and 1.4826*MAD at 3.88.
verified_values.knn_cannot_separate_dense: At k = 20 the tight cluster's kNN distances have median 0.27, the loose cluster's median 1.30, and the three planted strays sit at 1.22, 2.97 and 1.84 — so no global kNN threshold catches all three strays without also flagging half the loose cluster.
verified_values.lof_can: At k = 20 LOF has median 1.10 on the tight cluster and 1.04 on the loose one (95th percentiles 1.44 and 1.69), while the strays sit at 3.46, 3.52 and 5.19. A threshold of 2 catches all three and nothing else.
verified_values.mahalanobis_flips_the_order: On 'ellip', the point along the ridge is Euclidean-distance 4.58 from the mean but Mahalanobis 2.28; the point across the ridge is Euclidean 1.98 but Mahalanobis 3.98. The two rules disagree about which point is the outlier, and Mahalanobis is right.
verified_values.ring_boundary: At nu = 0.1, gamma = 0.5 the level set has an inner wall near r = 1.05-1.32 and an outer wall near r = 2.91-3.09, and all 8 planted points fall outside it. On the simply connected 'blob' the inner wall is 0.
verified_values.eval_curves: AUC-ROC = 0.9252, average precision = 0.7955. At threshold 0.5: TP 21, FP 4, FN 11, TN 364 — precision 0.840, recall 0.656, accuracy 0.963. Always predicting 'normal' scores accuracy 0.920, which is the point.
verified_values.base_rate_collapse: adPrecBayes(0.8, 0.05, 0.08) = 0.5818; adPrecBayes(0.8, 0.05, 0.001) = 0.0158. Same detector, same ROC curve, 37x worse precision.
verified_values.distance_concentration: Relative contrast (dmax - dmin) / dmin on 120 uniform points: 29.10 at d = 2, 9.26 at d = 3, 4.24 at d = 5, 1.78 at d = 10, 0.96 at d = 20, 0.61 at d = 40, 0.44 at d = 64.

note: No function reads a slider, so none of the contracts below is required for the library to work — they are the slider IDs the shipped lesson uses and passes in as arguments. Functions clamp their index arguments, so an out-of-range row returns an edge value rather than NaN. Dataset tags are strings: an unknown tag degrades to a plain 100-point standard cluster rather than to NaN, so a typo is visible rather than silent.

functions.adN: adN(tag) — number of points in a dataset.
functions.adX: adX(tag, i) — x of point i.
functions.adY: adY(tag, i) — y of point i.
functions.adLabel: adLabel(tag, i) — 1 if point i was PLANTED as anomalous, else 0. Ground truth, not a verdict.
functions.adMetricN: adMetricN() — 60, the length of the 1-D metric series.
functions.adV: adV(i, contam) — reading i of the metric with `contam` outliers injected.
functions.adPlanted: adPlanted(i, contam) — 1 if reading i is one of the `contam` planted outliers. Ground truth, so a scene can show what a rule MISSED and not only what it caught.
functions.adStdV: adStdV(contam) — sample standard deviation, n-1 denominator. Breakdown point 0.
functions.adMadV: adMadV(contam) — median absolute deviation from the median.
functions.adSigmaHat: adSigmaHat(contam) — 1.4826 * MAD, the robust estimate of sigma.
functions.adZv: adZv(i, contam) — the classical z-score (v - mean) / sd. Breakdown point 0 in BOTH estimators: one point sent to infinity takes the mean with it, and the sd moves quadratically faster, so the fence it defines RETREATS past the very reading that moved it. That is masking, and it is what adModZv fixes.
functions.adModZv: adModZv(i, contam) — the modified z-score (v - median) / (1.4826 MAD). Both estimators have breakdown point 1/2, so up to half the sample can be corrupted before it moves arbitrarily. The 1.4826 is 1/Phi^-1(0.75), the constant that makes 1.4826 MAD consistent for sigma under normality -- without it the scale is right in spirit and 32.6% low, since MAD converges to Phi^-1(0.75) sigma = 0.6745 sigma.
functions.adFenceZ: adFenceZ(side, k, contam) — mean + side*k*sd. side +1 upper, -1 lower.
functions.adFenceT: adFenceT(side, w, contam) — Tukey fence Q3 + w*IQR or Q1 - w*IQR; w = 1.5 is the usual whisker.
functions.adCountZ: adCountZ(k, contam) — readings the k-sigma z-rule flags.
functions.adCountM: adCountM(k, contam) — readings the k-sigma MAD rule flags.
functions.adCountT: adCountT(w, contam) — readings the Tukey rule flags.
functions.adGrubbs: adGrubbs(contam) — Grubbs' statistic G = max_i |v_i - mean| / s, the largest absolute z-score in the sample; the test statistic for 'is the most extreme point an outlier'. Watch it go the WRONG way as contamination rises: more outliers inflate s faster than they extend the numerator, so G falls from 5.32 at contam 1 to 3.62 at contam 8. A hypothesis test built on non-robust estimators is masked exactly like the rule it formalises.
functions.adKnn: adKnn(tag, i, k) — distance from point i to its k-th nearest neighbour (not the mean of the k; see adKnnMean). The simplest density proxy: large means the k-th neighbour is far, so the neighbourhood is sparse. It is an ABSOLUTE distance in feature units, which is its weakness -- when clusters differ in density, a normal point of the loose cluster scores higher than a genuine stray near the tight one, and no single threshold separates them. That failure is what adLof's ratio fixes.
functions.adKnnMean: adKnnMean(tag, i, k) — mean distance to the k nearest neighbours. Same idea as adKnn but averaged, so it is less jumpy when the k-th neighbour happens to sit on a gap. Same absolute-units weakness.
functions.adLof: adLof(tag, i, k) — Local Outlier Factor (Breunig et al., 2000). Asks whether i sits in a SPARSER place than its own neighbours do, which is not the same as being far from anything. Four steps. (1) k-distance(j) = distance from j to its k-th nearest neighbour. (2) Reachability: reach_k(i,j) = max(k-distance(j), d(i,j)) — a floor that stops one very close pair from exploding the density estimate. (3) Local reachability density: lrd(i) = k / sum_j reach_k(i,j) over the k nearest j. (4) LOF(i) = mean_j lrd(j) / lrd(i) — my neighbours' density divided by mine. ~1 means as crowded as its neighbourhood; >> 1 means locally sparse; < 1 means denser than its neighbours. Being a RATIO is the whole point: the absolute density of a region cancels, so a loose cluster and a tight one both score ~1 where adKnn would call every loose-cluster point an outlier. k is the bias -- below ~10 it is noisy, above the size of the smallest real cluster 'local' stops meaning anything.
functions.adMahal: adMahal(tag, i) — Mahalanobis distance from the SAMPLE mean, in the covariance metric: sqrt( (x-mu)^T S^-1 (x-mu) ), computed from the closed-form inverse of the 2x2 S. It is Euclidean distance after whitening, so it accounts for correlation and unequal variance -- an elongated cloud gets elliptical contours instead of circular ones (compare adEuclid). Two things it cannot do, both visible in this lesson: its contours are ELLIPSES, so it cannot exclude a hole (on 'ring' the points planted at the centre score as the most normal in the data), and mu and S are themselves estimated from contaminated data, so the outliers help define the metric that is supposed to catch them. MCD / Elliptic Envelope is the robust fix.
functions.adEuclid: adEuclid(tag, i) — plain Euclidean distance from the sample mean. Present as the control for adMahal: on a correlated cloud the two disagree about which points are extreme, and the checker pins that they reverse each other's order.
functions.adCovEig: adCovEig(tag, which, s) — the covariance ellipse: which 0 angle in radians, 1 semi-major, 2 semi-minor, 3 mean x, 4 mean y; s scales the axes (s = 2 is the 2-sigma contour).
functions.adEllipse: adEllipse(tag, theta, s, axis) — a point on the s-sigma covariance ellipse at parameter theta; axis 0 = x, 1 = y. The form an animated_polygon's vertices want.
functions.adConc: adConc(d, which) — distance concentration in d dimensions, measured on 120 seeded uniform points: which 0 the relative contrast (dmax - dmin) / dmin averaged over points, 1 the mean nearest distance, 2 the mean farthest. The curse of dimensionality, as a number rather than an assertion.
functions.adCPath: adCPath(n) — c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n, the expected unsuccessful-search path length in a BST of n nodes. H is summed exactly (memoised prefix); the ln+gamma asymptotic is used only above n = 100000.
functions.adIsoDepth: adIsoDepth(tag, x, y) — mean isolation path length over the forest at an ARBITRARY point, not only at a data point, which is what lets the heatmap score the whole plane. Walks all 100 trees; a node that ran out of depth or points credits c(size) for the subtree it did not build, which is Liu's estimator. Memoised on the exact coordinate pair.
functions.adIsoGrid: adIsoGrid(tag, x, y) — the Isolation Forest score 2^(-E[h]/c(psi)) at an arbitrary point. Near 1 isolated, near 0.5 ordinary.
functions.adIso: adIso(tag, i) — the Isolation Forest score at data point i, i.e. adIsoGrid evaluated at that point's coordinates. s = 2^(-E[h(x)]/c(psi)) in (0,1): s -> 1 means isolated in very few cuts, s ~ 0.5 means an ordinary point (E[h] = c(psi) exactly), s -> 0 means it took far longer than average to isolate.
functions.adKde: adKde(tag, x, y, gamma) — Gaussian RBF kernel sum, (1/n) sum_j exp(-gamma ||x - x_j||^2). NOT a normalised density: a 2-D Gaussian kernel needs a further factor gamma/pi, so this integrates to pi/gamma rather than 1. That is deliberate and harmless here, because the boundary compares this against a quantile OF THE SAME quantity and the constant cancels exactly -- but it is proportional to a KDE, not one. gamma is the inverse-square bandwidth: large gamma = narrow kernels = the estimate memorises individual points.
functions.adKdeScore: adKdeScore(tag, i, gamma) — the density at training point i, cached per (tag, gamma).
functions.adKdeQ: adKdeQ(tag, nu, gamma) — the nu-quantile of the training points' OWN densities; the one-class decision threshold. Quantiling the training scores is what turns nu into something operational -- declare everything below it an outlier and you reject approximately nu of the training set (0.101 at nu = 0.1 on 'ring'). Approximately, not exactly: it is an interpolated empirical quantile and the membership test keeps ties. This is an operational analogue of a nu-SVM's nu, not the same guarantee; there nu bounds the training-error fraction above and the support-vector fraction below.
functions.adKdeIn: adKdeIn(tag, i, nu, gamma) — 1 when training point i is inside the one-class boundary, 0 when it is rejected.
functions.adKdeR: adKdeR(tag, theta, nu, gamma, rMax) — radius of the OUTER boundary crossing along the ray at angle theta.
functions.adKdeRin: adKdeRin(tag, theta, nu, gamma, rMax) — radius of the INNER crossing (an annulus's hole); 0 for a simply connected region.
functions.adKdeB: adKdeB(tag, theta, nu, gamma, axis, wall) — x or y of the boundary point; axis 0 = x, 1 = y; wall 0 = outer, 1 = inner.
functions.adSigN: adSigN() — 128, the length of the signal.
functions.adSig: adSig(i) — the signal at sample i.
functions.adSigLabel: adSigLabel(i) — 1 inside the planted collective anomaly (samples 74-82).
functions.adRecon: adRecon(i, r) — the rank-r reconstruction at sample i (mean plus the r lowest Fourier modes).
functions.adResid: adResid(i, r) — |signal - reconstruction| at sample i; the anomaly score.
functions.adReconRmse: adReconRmse(r) — RMSE over the whole signal. Falls monotonically with capacity.
functions.adReconRmseAnom: adReconRmseAnom(r) — RMSE restricted to the planted window. When this falls as fast as adReconRmse, the model has learned the anomaly and the detector is dead.
functions.adPcaErr: adPcaErr(tag, i) — distance from point i to the first principal axis, i.e. |the component ACROSS the major axis| after rotating into the covariance eigenbasis. This is the reconstruction error of a rank-1 linear model: what you lose by describing the cloud with one direction. The linear ancestor of the autoencoder error in scene 5, and the reason that scene opens with PCA before anything is learned.
functions.adPcaSurf: adPcaSurf(tag, x, y) — the squared version of that error as a surface over the plane.
functions.adScore: adScore(i) — the i-th score of the labelled evaluation set, sorted descending.
functions.adConf: adConf(t, cell) — confusion count at threshold t, flagging when score >= t. cell 0 TP, 1 FP, 2 FN, 3 TN. The scores are held sorted descending, so the count is a prefix scan rather than a pass over the data. Everything else in scene 6 -- adTpr, adFpr, adPrec, the curves -- is a ratio of these four numbers, which is why they are exposed individually.
functions.adTpr: adTpr(t) — true positive rate at threshold t: TP / P, the fraction of the ACTUAL ANOMALIES that get flagged. It conditions on the truth, so it is measured only among the positives and the class mix cannot move it. That is what makes it a property of the detector. Also called recall and sensitivity (adRec is an alias).
functions.adFpr: adFpr(t) — false positive rate at threshold t: FP / N, the fraction of the ACTUAL NORMALS wrongly flagged. Conditions on the truth like adTpr, so it is also a property of the detector. Note N is usually enormous in a real problem, so a tiny FPR still produces most of your alerts -- that is the arithmetic behind adPrecBayes.
functions.adRec: adRec(t) — recall; an alias of adTpr, present so a PR curve can be written in the names it is usually drawn with.
functions.adPrec: adPrec(t) — precision at threshold t: TP / (TP + FP), the fraction of the ALERTS that are real. Unlike adTpr and adFpr it conditions on the ALERT, not on the truth, so it cannot be computed without the base rate and it is NOT a property of the detector -- the same detector has different precision on a rarer population. Returns 1 when nothing is flagged, which is the usual convention and worth knowing before reading the top of a PR curve.
functions.adAcc: adAcc(t) — accuracy, (TP + TN) / n. Present so the lesson can show it staying high while the detector is useless: with a 1% base rate, always predicting 'normal' scores 99% and finds nothing. Never report it for an anomaly problem.
functions.adFlagged: adFlagged(t) — how many points are flagged at all; the alert volume.
functions.adPrecAtK: adPrecAtK(k) — precision among the top k scores: of the k highest-ranked points, how many are real. This is the metric that matches how detectors are actually run, because k is an alert budget -- how many items a human can look at in a day -- and not a probability threshold anyone chose.
functions.adRocX: adRocX(i, n) — FPR of the i-th of n operating points, swept by rank.
functions.adRocY: adRocY(i, n) — TPR of the same point.
functions.adPrX: adPrX(i, n) — recall of the i-th of n operating points.
functions.adPrY: adPrY(i, n) — precision of the same point.
functions.adAucRoc: adAucRoc() — area under the ROC curve, by the trapezoid rule over every distinct operating point. Reads as the probability that a random anomaly is ranked above a random normal, so it is threshold-free and, because both axes condition on the truth, INSENSITIVE TO THE BASE RATE. That invariance is the trap: it scores only anomaly-vs-normal PAIRS, and that pairwise ranking probability does not move when the class proportions do -- so it stays flattering under heavy imbalance while the operator drowns, because the COUNT of false positives grows with the number of normals even though the ranking statistic is unchanged. It can also hide a bimodal failure -- a detector that ranks half the anomalies first and half last averages to 0.5, the same number as chance. Pair it with adAucPr.
functions.adAucPr: adAucPr() — average precision, the PR-curve summary. Unlike adAucRoc it DOES move with the base rate, which is the point: its floor is the contamination rate rather than 0.5, so it reports what an operator experiences. It is the metric to lead with under imbalance, and the one that separates detectors that adAucRoc calls nearly identical.
functions.adPrecBayes: adPrecBayes(tpr, fpr, pi) — precision = TPR pi / (TPR pi + FPR (1 - pi)), i.e. Bayes' theorem with the two rates the detector controls on one side and the base rate on the other. PURE: it consults no dataset, so a scene can sweep pi and watch precision collapse for a FIXED detector. As pi -> 0, precision ~ (TPR/FPR) pi -> 0 for any detector that ever produces a false positive.
functions.adFalseAlarms: adFalseAlarms(fpr, pi, volume) — expected false alarms per period.
functions.adDetAuc: adDetAuc(datasetIdx, detectorIdx) — AUC-ROC of one detector on one dataset, by the Mann-Whitney identity: the probability that a random planted point outranks a random normal one, ties counting a half. datasetIdx 0 blob, 1 dense, 2 ring -- ordered by what they BREAK (one convex cloud, two densities, a hole). detectorIdx 0 isolation, 1 LOF, 2 kNN, 3 kernel density, 4 Mahalanobis; kernel density is sign-flipped internally since low density is the anomalous case. Computed live rather than pinned into the scene, so the no-free-lunch matrix cannot drift from the detectors it claims to score. O(P*N) per cell, cached per pair -- 15 cells built once, not per frame.

contam.description: How many of the 60 metric readings are replaced by large ones, 0 to 8. Passed to every scene-2 function. The outliers come from a fixed list in a fixed order, so raising the slider adds one and disturbs none.

kz.description: The fence width in standard deviations, shared by the z-rule and the MAD rule so the two are compared at the same k. 2 to 5.

k.description: Neighbourhood size for adKnn and adLof, 2 to 40. Below about 10 LOF is noisy; above the size of the smallest real cluster it stops being local.

nu.description: Target fraction of the training data the one-class boundary rejects, 0.01 to 0.4. The cutoff is an interpolated empirical quantile of the training points' own densities and `>=` keeps ties, so the realised rejection is APPROXIMATELY nu (nu = 0.1 rejects 0.101 of the 'ring' set). This is not the nu of a nu-SVM, where nu upper-bounds the training-error fraction and lower-bounds the support-vector fraction; the analogy is operational, and this is not an SVM.

gamma.description: RBF kernel width parameter, 0.05 to 3. Small gamma gives a smooth, nearly convex boundary; large gamma lets the boundary shrink-wrap every point and memorise the training set.

rank.description: Reconstruction capacity r: how many Fourier modes the model may keep, 1 to 32. The whole capacity argument lives on this slider.

thr.description: Score threshold for the evaluation sweep, 0 to 1. Everything scoring at or above it is flagged.

pi.description: Base rate — the true fraction of anomalies in the population, 0.0005 to 0.2, for the adPrecBayes identity. The detector's TPR and FPR are held fixed while this moves.

MAD.markdown:
$\mathrm{MAD} = \operatorname{median}_i \lvert x_i - \operatorname{median}(x)\rvert$

A robust spread: scaled by $1.4826$ it estimates $\sigma$ for Gaussian data, yet a handful of wild points barely move it — its **breakdown point** is 50%.
MAD.prompt: Explain the median absolute deviation (MAD): how it is computed, why it is scaled by 1.4826, and why it resists outliers where the standard deviation does not.

breakdown point.markdown: The largest fraction of the data that can be replaced by arbitrary values before an estimator can be dragged arbitrarily far. The mean's is $0\%$; the median's and MAD's is $50\%$.
breakdown point.prompt: Explain the breakdown point of an estimator, and compare the mean, the standard deviation, the median and the MAD.

z-score.markdown: $z = \dfrac{x - \bar x}{s}$ — how many standard deviations a point sits from the mean. Both $\bar x$ and $s$ are pulled by the very outliers it is meant to flag.
z-score.prompt: Explain the z-score as an outlier test and why masking makes it fail when the outliers themselves inflate the mean and standard deviation.

kNN.markdown: The distance from a point to its $k$-th nearest neighbour. Large means isolated — but only relative to a single global scale, which is why it struggles when clusters have different densities.
kNN.prompt: Explain the k-th nearest neighbour distance as an anomaly score, how k is chosen, and where it fails on data with clusters of different density.

LOF.markdown: The ratio of a point's neighbours' local reachability density to its own. $\mathrm{LOF}\approx 1$ means as dense as its neighbourhood; $\mathrm{LOF}\gg 1$ means locally sparse, whatever the global scale.
LOF.prompt: Explain the Local Outlier Factor: reachability distance, local reachability density, and why the ratio adapts to clusters of different density.

Mahalanobis.markdown: $d_M(x) = \sqrt{(x-\mu)^\top \Sigma^{-1} (x-\mu)}$ — distance measured in the data's own covariance, so its level sets are ellipses aligned with the spread.
Mahalanobis.prompt: Explain the Mahalanobis distance, why it uses the inverse covariance, and how outliers contaminate the covariance estimate it depends on.

Isolation Forest.markdown: Random axis-aligned splits isolate a point; anomalies take fewer splits. The score normalises the mean path length by $c(n)$, the average path of an unsuccessful BST search.
Isolation Forest.prompt: Explain how an Isolation Forest scores anomalies by path length, and what the c(n) normalisation is for.

RBF.markdown:
$k_\gamma(x,x') = e^{-\gamma\lVert x-x'\rVert^2}$

A **choice**, not a result — it asserts that nearness is radial and means the same thing everywhere. That is an inductive bias.
RBF.prompt: Explain the Gaussian RBF kernel: what it assumes, why isotropy and a single bandwidth are an inductive bias, and when that bias is wrong.

SVM.markdown: Finds a boundary in kernel feature space that encloses most of the data; $\nu$ upper-bounds the fraction of training points left outside.
SVM.prompt: Explain the one-class SVM: what the boundary means, the role of nu, and how the kernel bandwidth gamma shapes it.

ROC.markdown: True-positive rate against false-positive rate as the threshold sweeps. Blind to the base rate, so it can look excellent where precision is poor.
ROC.prompt: Explain the ROC curve and AUC, and why they can look excellent on a rare-positive problem where precision is poor.

AUC.markdown: The probability that a random positive outscores a random negative. Threshold-free — and base-rate-free, which is both its strength and its trap.
AUC.prompt: Explain ROC AUC as a ranking probability and why it ignores the base rate.

base rate.markdown: The fraction of cases that are truly positive. At a low base rate even a small false-positive rate swamps the true positives, so precision collapses.
base rate.prompt: Explain the base rate and why a low base rate makes precision collapse even for a detector with a small false-positive rate.

Tukey's fences.markdown: Flag $v < Q_1 - k\,\mathrm{IQR}$ or $v > Q_3 + k\,\mathrm{IQR}$, with $k = 1.5$ for an outlier and $k = 3$ for a far-out one. Built from quartiles, so it needs no mean or standard deviation.
Tukey's fences.prompt: Explain Tukey's fences: how the quartiles and the IQR set them, why k is 1.5 or 3, and how robust they are compared with a z-score rule.

IQR.markdown: $\mathrm{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$ — the spread of the middle half of the data. Like the MAD it ignores the tails, so a few extreme points cannot inflate it.
IQR.prompt: Explain the interquartile range and why it is a robust measure of spread.

Grubbs' test.markdown: $G = \max_i \lvert v_i - \bar v\rvert / s$, compared with a critical value from the $t$ distribution. It assumes normal data and tests for **one** outlier; repeated or generalized versions (ESD) test for several.
Grubbs' test.prompt: Explain Grubbs' test: the statistic, its normality assumption, and why it suffers from masking when there are several outliers.

masking.markdown: Outliers inflate the scale estimate (and shift the centre) until they fall inside their own fence, so the rule stops seeing them.
masking.prompt: Explain masking in outlier detection with an example, and how robust estimators avoid it.

swamping.markdown: The mirror of masking: the same contaminated estimates push ordinary points outside the fence, so good data gets flagged.
swamping.prompt: Explain swamping in outlier detection and how it relates to masking.

autoencoder.markdown: A model trained to reconstruct its input through a narrow bottleneck. Points unlike the training data reconstruct badly, so the **reconstruction error** serves as an anomaly score.
autoencoder.prompt: Explain how an autoencoder is used for anomaly detection and what the bottleneck forces it to learn.

reconstruction error.markdown: $\lVert x - \hat x\rVert^2$, the distance between a point and its reconstruction from a low-rank or learned code. Large means the model's picture of normal data does not fit the point.
reconstruction error.prompt: Explain reconstruction error as an anomaly score, for PCA and for autoencoders, and where it fails.

ESD.markdown: Rosner's generalized extreme Studentized deviate test. For $i = 1..r$ it removes the most extreme point and computes $R_i = \max\lvert v - \bar v\rvert / s$ on what remains, comparing each with a critical value $\lambda_i$. The number of outliers is the largest $i$ with $R_i > \lambda_i$, which resists the masking that sinks a single Grubbs' test.
ESD.prompt: Explain the generalized ESD test: how it iterates, how the critical values are set, and why it handles several outliers better than repeated Grubbs' tests.

FPR.markdown: $\mathrm{FPR} = \dfrac{FP}{FP + TN}$ — the fraction of normal points that get flagged. The $x$-axis of the ROC curve.
FPR.prompt: Explain the false-positive rate, and why a small FPR can still mean most alerts are false when anomalies are rare.

TPR.markdown: $\mathrm{TPR} = \dfrac{TP}{TP + FN}$ — the fraction of real anomalies that get flagged. Also called recall or sensitivity; the $y$-axis of the ROC curve.
TPR.prompt: Explain the true-positive rate (recall) and how it trades off against the false-positive rate as the threshold moves.

PR curve.markdown: Precision against recall as the threshold sweeps. Unlike ROC it depends on the base rate: a random detector sits at precision $=$ base rate, so it shows the cost of rare positives honestly.
PR curve.prompt: Explain the precision-recall curve, why its baseline is the base rate, and when to prefer it over ROC.

PR-AUC.markdown: Summarises the precision–recall curve in one number (often computed as **average precision**). Its chance level is the base rate, not $0.5$.
PR-AUC.prompt: Explain PR-AUC or average precision, and why its chance level is the base rate.

BST.markdown: In Isolation Forest, $c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n$ is the average path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree of $n$ points ($H$ is the harmonic number). It normalises path lengths so scores are comparable across sample sizes.
BST.prompt: Explain why Isolation Forest normalises path length by the average unsuccessful-search depth of a binary search tree, c(n).

RMSE.markdown: $\sqrt{\tfrac{1}{d}\sum_j (x_j - \hat x_j)^2}$ — the typical size of a reconstruction or forecast error, in the data's own units.
RMSE.prompt: Explain RMSE and how it is used as a reconstruction-error anomaly score.

VAE.markdown: An autoencoder whose code is a probability distribution. Anomalies can be scored by reconstruction error or by the model's likelihood bound (ELBO) — though likelihoods can rank out-of-distribution data as *more* probable.
VAE.prompt: Explain how a variational autoencoder is used for anomaly detection and the pitfalls of likelihood-based scores.

OOD.markdown: Data not drawn from the distribution a model was trained on. Out-of-distribution detection is anomaly detection applied to a model's inputs.
OOD.prompt: Explain out-of-distribution detection and how it relates to anomaly detection.

STL.markdown: Splits a series into trend $+$ seasonal $+$ remainder using local regression. Anomalies are scored on the remainder, so a reading that is normal for its season is not flagged.
STL.prompt: Explain STL decomposition and how its remainder is used to find time-series anomalies.

ARIMA.markdown: Autoregressive integrated moving-average model — a classical linear forecaster. For anomaly detection its **forecast residual** is the score.
ARIMA.prompt: Explain how an ARIMA forecast is used to detect anomalies in a time series.

LSTM.markdown: A recurrent neural network that can carry information across long sequences. Used as a learned forecaster (score the residual) or as a sequence autoencoder.
LSTM.prompt: Explain how LSTM networks are used for time-series anomaly detection.

MCD.markdown: Finds the $h$ points whose covariance matrix has the smallest determinant and estimates centre and scatter from them. A robust replacement for the mean and covariance, so the Mahalanobis distance it feeds is not masked by the outliers it hunts.
MCD.prompt: Explain the minimum covariance determinant estimator and why it makes Mahalanobis distance robust.

elliptic envelope.markdown: Fit a robust Gaussian (via MCD) and flag points whose robust Mahalanobis distance is too large — an ellipse drawn around the bulk of the data.
elliptic envelope.prompt: Explain the elliptic envelope outlier detector and its assumptions.

LSCP.term: Locally Selective Combination of Parallel outlier ensembles
LSCP.markdown: Runs many detectors, and for each test point picks the ones that agree best with a pseudo ground truth in its local region, instead of averaging them all.
LSCP.prompt: Explain LSCP and why selecting detectors locally can beat averaging an ensemble.

COF.markdown: A LOF variant that measures density along chaining paths rather than spheres, so points on a sparse line or curve are not mistaken for outliers.
COF.prompt: Explain the connectivity-based outlier factor and how it differs from LOF.

INFLO.markdown: A LOF variant whose neighbourhood includes reverse nearest neighbours (points that count *this* point as a neighbour), which helps where clusters of different density touch.
INFLO.prompt: Explain INFLO and why reverse nearest neighbours help at the border between clusters.

DBSCAN.markdown: Density-based clustering: points with enough neighbours within $\varepsilon$ form clusters, and points reachable from none are labelled **noise** — a built-in outlier label.
DBSCAN.prompt: Explain DBSCAN and how its noise points act as outliers, including how eps and minPts matter.

SVDD.markdown: The smallest sphere in kernel feature space that encloses most of the data; points outside are anomalies. With a Gaussian kernel it is equivalent to the one-class SVM.
SVDD.prompt: Explain support vector data description and its relation to the one-class SVM.

DeepSVDD.markdown: A neural network trained to map normal data close to a fixed centre $c$; the anomaly score is the distance $\lVert\phi(x) - c\rVert$. Needs care to stop the network collapsing everything onto $c$.
DeepSVDD.prompt: Explain Deep SVDD, its training objective, and the collapse problem.

DeepSAD.markdown: Semi-supervised Deep SVDD: a few labelled anomalies are pushed *away* from the centre while unlabelled data is pulled toward it.
DeepSAD.prompt: Explain Deep SAD and how a few labelled anomalies improve Deep SVDD.

extended isolation forest.markdown: Isolation Forest with random-slope hyperplane splits instead of axis-parallel ones, which removes the axis-aligned artefacts in the score map.
extended isolation forest.prompt: Explain the Extended Isolation Forest and the artefacts of axis-parallel splits it fixes.

feature bagging.markdown: Run a detector (often LOF) on many random subsets of the features and combine the scores, so an anomaly visible in only a few dimensions is not drowned out.
feature bagging.prompt: Explain feature bagging for outlier detection and why it helps in high dimensions.

subspace methods.markdown: Look for outliers in lower-dimensional projections of the data. In high dimensions distances concentrate, so an anomaly may only stand out in a few features.
subspace methods.prompt: Explain subspace outlier detection and the concentration of distances in high dimensions.

random projections.markdown: Project the data onto random low-dimensional subspaces; by the Johnson–Lindenstrauss lemma pairwise distances are roughly preserved, making distance-based detectors cheaper.
random projections.prompt: Explain random projections and why they preserve distances well enough for outlier detection.

forecast residual.markdown: Observed value minus a model's forecast. A point is anomalous when the residual is large relative to the residuals' usual spread.
forecast residual.prompt: Explain forecast-residual anomaly detection and how the threshold on residuals is set.

spectral residual.markdown: A saliency method for time series: subtract a smoothed log-amplitude spectrum from the actual one and transform back; spikes in the result mark anomalies.
spectral residual.prompt: Explain the spectral residual method for time-series anomaly detection.

matrix profile.markdown: For each subsequence of a time series, the distance to its nearest non-overlapping match. A high value is a **discord** — a shape that occurs nowhere else.
matrix profile.prompt: Explain the matrix profile and how discords reveal time-series anomalies.

point anomaly.markdown: A single observation that is unusual on its own, whatever its context.
point anomaly.prompt: Explain point anomalies and give examples.

contextual anomaly.markdown: A value that is normal globally but unusual in its context — $30^\circ$C is ordinary in July and anomalous in January.
contextual anomaly.prompt: Explain contextual anomalies and how context features change detection.

collective anomaly.markdown: A group of observations that is anomalous together although each point looks normal on its own — a flat stretch in a signal that should oscillate.
collective anomaly.prompt: Explain collective anomalies and why point-wise detectors miss them.

inductive bias.markdown: The assumptions a method brings before seeing data — what it treats as near, smooth or simple. Every detector has one; it decides which anomalies it can see.
inductive bias.prompt: Explain inductive bias in anomaly detection with examples from distance, density and kernel methods.

isotropy.markdown: Looking the same in every direction. An isotropic kernel depends only on $\lVert x - x'\rVert$, so it treats all feature directions alike.
isotropy.prompt: Explain isotropy for a kernel and when that assumption fails.

stationarity.markdown: For a kernel: depending only on $x - x'$, not on where you are — the same notion of nearness everywhere. For a time series: statistics that do not change over time.
stationarity.prompt: Explain stationarity, both for kernels and for time series, and why anomaly detectors often assume it.

contamination.markdown: The fraction of the data that is anomalous. Many detectors take it as a parameter to set their threshold, which quietly encodes a guess about the base rate.
contamination.prompt: Explain the contamination parameter in anomaly detectors and what setting it implies.

active learning.markdown: Ask a human to label the points the model is least sure about, so a few labels improve the detector as much as possible.
active learning.prompt: Explain active learning for anomaly detection and how to choose which points to label.

drift.markdown: The distribution of normal data changes over time, so a model or threshold fitted in the past starts flagging the new normal — or missing the new abnormal.
drift.prompt: Explain data drift and concept drift, and how to keep an anomaly detector calibrated.

whitening.markdown: The linear map $z = \Sigma^{-1/2}(x - \mu)$. It rescales each principal axis of the data by its own standard deviation, so the whitened data has identity covariance and the ellipse becomes a circle. Euclidean distance on $z$ **is** the Mahalanobis distance on $x$.
whitening.prompt: Explain whitening: what the map Sigma^(-1/2)(x - mu) does geometrically, why the whitened data has identity covariance, and why Euclidean distance after whitening equals the Mahalanobis distance.
